A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 21 vision encoders, including synthetic binding results, geometric and Jacobian correlations, readout comparisons, and robustness analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 26 encoders, retains the synthetic experiments, and adds SugarCrepe validation, initialization controls, and further diagnostic comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 adds a null-calibrated diagnostic variant, ΔJER = JERtrained − JERnull, requiring measurements of trained and randomly initialized instances of the same architecture (Section 4.2 and Appendix C). The underlying Jacobian-spectrum estimator and original JER formula remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds natural-image compositional evaluation on SugarCrepe: 7,511 image–caption trials covering seven addition, replacement, and swap subtypes. This substantially extends the original synthetic shape–position binding coverage. The synthetic binding and Same/Different tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes SimCLR and both I-JEPA entries and adds eight encoders, including MoCo v3, supervised ViT-B/L, and larger DINOv2, ConvNeXt, SigLIP, and EVA-CLIP variants. v2 also evaluates random-initialization comparators and linear CKA/Procrustes geometric comparators absent from v1.

E3.justification: Primary JER evaluation changes from Gaussian noise to ImageNet validation images, with noise retained as a control. New protocols include SugarCrepe caption ranking and scoring schemes, matched initialization comparisons, and pairwise geometry on 200 binding stimuli. Architectural controls change from parameter count to log parameter count. Section 3.1 also changes local-isotropy k from 16 to 32, although v2 Table 13 still lists 16.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether JER reflects training rather than initialization, whether its association survives natural-versus-noise inputs, and whether geometric diagnostics fail on matched noise inputs. SugarCrepe analyses control for ImageNet accuracy and architecture, while Appendix D tests inter-model shape distances. Existing readout, qualitative, and local-isotropy analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds Mantel significance tests with 10,000 permutations and Spearman correlations. It removes the reported jackknife influence check in which 19/21 samples retained significance. Five-seed noise-JER means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, and regression LOO-CV remain; no increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Under the revised encoder suite and primary JER input domain, Table 2 replaces the JER–binding correlation of 0.65 with 0.69 and combined-predictor LOO-CV R² of 0.65 with 0.71. These are not same-setting gains; retained encoders' binding accuracies remain unchanged. Substantial new results include SugarCrepe correlation r=0.69, p=0.009, initialization calibration, shape-distance null results, noise controls, and computational costs.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces the mathematical definition of the null-calibrated quantity ΔJER. The original JER definition, augmentation expansion, and objective-specific derivations are otherwise retained, with v1 Appendix B becoming v2 Appendix G. No new proof replaces the original theoretical account.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: global geometric diagnostics inadequately predict binding, functional sensitivity provides complementary information, and objective design explains sensitivity differences. Expanded experiments and the revised encoder count strengthen the evidence without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets initialization controls as evidence that training reduces functional rank and explains inter-model variation. It extends applicability to natural-image compositional evaluation within the CLIP-family scope. Appendix A.1 adds substantive cautions about off-manifold probes, the modest model sample and sparse objective families, and tasks where global geometry remains informative.

D1.justification: v2 expands checkpoint, source, and embedding-dimension documentation; newly specifies five power iterations; and adds A6000 timing comparisons in Appendix F. Appendix I resolves v1's conflicting 20-versus-100-image JER averaging descriptions in favor of 100, without establishing an actual sample-count increase. Code release remains planned in both versions.

R1.justification: v2 adds cognitive-science binding references, the SugarCrepe citation, and a focused discussion of inter-model representational similarity involving Kornblith, Williams, Bo, and Braun. This broadens the relevant comparison literature while retaining the original positioning around limitations of static geometric diagnostics.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds contextual explanations, clarifies the Same/Different distinction and rank-collapse narrative, inserts natural-image validation before the retained readout analyses, and expands the appendix overview. Original appendices B–E become G–J rather than being removed.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with SugarCrepe, 26-model null-calibration, and computational-cost tables, plus compact shape-distance and noise-control tables. Tables 2 and 3 gain rows, and Figure 1 is updated for the revised results. Figures 2–6 retain their content despite relocation; the overall visual style remains stable.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence relied on synthetic binding and noise-based JER. v2 substantially strengthens validity through natural-image JER, SugarCrepe validation, and initialization and matched-input controls that address generalization and confounding concerns. Added limitations and timing information improve interpretation and practical assessment. CLIP-only natural-image validation and reporting inconsistencies, such as the conflicting local-isotropy k settings, remain limitations but do not outweigh these gains.
